To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

increasing the size of the data set often results in a proportional increase in decision tree size, that this increase is not always accompanied by a corresponding increase in accuracy, and that a substantial portion of the eectiveness of data reduction techniques can be attributed to the fact that they reduce the size of the dataset.

(1) increasing the training set size often increases tree size linearly, even when that increased complexity results in no increase in accuracy, (2) the size of trees built by c4.5 is often substantially smaller when built with random subsamples of the training set, and (3) a large percentage of the reduction in tree size due to John's robust-c5.5 is due to its reduction in training set size, not its selection of which instances to discard.

the following question: What is the relationship between tree complexity and training set size?

the training set size has a direct effect on the complexity of decision trees and that this relationship is not linear.

the size of the decision tree is not a useful metric for measuring the performance of data reduction techniques.
